idiom_name: recursive generic bound for self-typed APIs; inline functions with reified type parameters for compile-time type access
implementation_notes: Kotlin can express the CRTP structure with a recursive bound - abstract class Base<T : Base<T>> with an abstract accessor returning T - but the JVM gives it no dispatch advantage: instance calls stay virtual and generic type arguments are erased. The two purposes CRTP serves are covered by other idioms: compile-time type access by inline functions with reified type parameters (the body is inlined at each call site, so is T, T::class and type-specific dispatch are available without reflection), and the mixin half by interface default implementations plus extension functions. Use a recursive bound when a fluent API must return the concrete receiver type; use inline/reified when the point is compile-time knowledge of a type.
code_sketch:
abstract class Builder<T : Builder<T>> {          // recursive bound
    protected abstract val self: T
    fun named(value: String): T = self
}

inline fun <reified T> List<*>.ofType(): List<T> = filterIsInstance<T>()
pitfalls: Reified type parameters exist only on inline functions, and inline functions cannot be recursive or mocked at the function level; outside that boundary a KClass token must be passed explicitly.
Generics are erased on the JVM, so this as T inside a recursive-bound base is an unchecked cast that can throw ClassCastException when the wrong type argument is bound.
Instance dispatch remains virtual, so a recursive-bound 'static polymorphism' base buys type safety and API shape only - do not choose it for performance.
